title: Growing Together and inclusionary zoning hearings
subtitle: Delegations heard on transit-area zoning and affordable housing rules; both decisions referred to the evening Council meeting.
overview: A special Council meeting heard from dozens of delegates on two major planning items: the Growing Together land use and zoning framework for seven Protected Major Transit Station Areas, and a new inclusionary zoning policy that would require some affordable units in new buildings in those areas.

Council did not decide either item at this meeting. Because of the number of delegations and the time they took, both recommendations were referred to the regular Council meeting later the same day {{vote:m2}} {{vote:m3}}. Council also agreed to hold a closed session on a legal matter and a personal matter about an identifiable individual {{vote:m1}}.

For residents, the outcome is still pending. Growing Together would change permitted building heights, uses and rules near the ION line, and inclusionary zoning would set initial affordable-unit rates that start low and are reviewed regularly. Staff also announced corrections to the Growing Together documents, which would apply if Council approves them. The meeting ended at 7:05 p.m.

decisions.detail: Council referred the proposed Official Plan amendments and zoning by-law amendments for seven transit station areas to the later Council meeting so it could deal with them there, given time constraints {{vote:m2}}.

Council referred the proposed inclusionary zoning Official Plan and zoning amendments, a memorandum of understanding with the Region, and market reviews through 2030 to the later Council meeting {{vote:m3}}.
Council authorized a closed session after the special meeting to consider solicitor-client privilege and a personal matter about an identifiable individual {{vote:m1}}.

debate: Supporters of Growing Together said the framework is overdue and would add housing near transit. A delegate said it should cover the whole city, and others said density supports community and affordability. Staff called it the most permissive zoning in Canada, with built-form rules for livability.

Residents and some planners raised concerns about the pace and scope of the plan, including late additions such as commercial uses in residential areas and the removal of secondary plans. Others raised heritage conservation, transitions between tall and low buildings, street trees, and construction impacts on older homes. Staff said they would continue construction-impact tools and street tree work, and that they did not see a need to keep deferring the secondary plans.

Developers and planning consultants asked for changes to specific properties, such as higher height zones, and one developer asked for larger floor plates and smaller setbacks for tall buildings. Staff said taller buildings already get different standards and that extra height could be sought through site-specific applications.

On inclusionary zoning, many delegates said the initial rates are too low and slow and asked for the 5% maximum sooner. Developer delegates said costs would be passed to first-time buyers and renters, and that market conditions remain difficult. Some said housing affordability is a government responsibility. Staff said the policy is flexible, offsets costs, and will be reviewed regularly.
Delegates for seniors and housing advocates raised displacement and renovictions, and a developer asked that an earlier affordable-housing commitment on a Victoria Street site be honoured.
